n: Museum of Contemporary History of Russia
funding: The museum is the Federal State Budgetary Institution of Culture State Central Museum of Contemporary History of Russia, a federal museum under the Ministry of Culture of the Russian Federation. It is funded from the federal budget as a state budgetary institution. It was the Museum of the Revolution of the USSR until 1998.
note: Housed in the former English Club mansion at Tverskaya 21; the 2022 exhibition NATO, Chronicle of Cruelty drew almost 20,000 visitors in under two months with free entry.

propaganda.summary: In April 2022 the museum opened NATO, Chronicle of Cruelty with Defense Ministry trophies from Ukraine; in 2024 it co-wrote the Culture Ministry's guidelines for special military operation exhibitions nationwide.

funding: The State Stalin Museum is a Georgian state museum funded and protected by the Ministry of Culture and Monuments of Georgia and listed as a cultural heritage monument. Its restoration tenders run through the State Procurement Agency. Director Lia Okroperidze heads the museum.
note: The 1957 complex by architect Archil Kurdiani holds about 40,000 items; Gori's tourist centre counted roughly 162,000 visitors in 2018, and a room on repressions was added in 2010.

propaganda.summary: Soviet authorities opened the museum complex in 1957, a year after Khrushchev's secret speech, as a monument honouring Stalin; a 2012 Georgian plan to refocus it on his atrocities was never carried out.

funding: The museum is a state institution of the Republic of Serbia: the Government of Serbia appoints its director and the Ministry of Culture must consent to director competitions under the Law on Culture. It was founded in 1996 by the Government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia by merging the Josip Broz Tito Memorial Centre and the Museum of the Revolution of Yugoslav Peoples. Entry is free.
note: About 100,000 to 120,000 visitors a year, the most visited museum in Serbia; the complex includes the 1962 building by Mihailo Janković and the House of Flowers, Tito's tomb.

propaganda.summary: The City of Belgrade built the museum in 1962 as a 70th birthday gift to Tito, to display and preserve the gifts he received; after his death in 1980 it became the Tito Memorial Centre.

funding: The museum is a state institution under Albania's Ministry of Economy, Culture and Innovation, which appoints its director. Its 2024 to 2028 reconstruction is funded from the state Public Investment programme (606 million lek) and the EU4Culture programme through UNOPS. It closed in March 2024 for four years of works.
note: The largest museum in Albania at 27,000 square metres, opened 28 October 1981 with the mosaic The Albanians on its facade; a Communist Terror pavilion was added in 2012.

propaganda.summary: Hoxha's regime built the museum from 1978 and opened it in 1981 with displays shaped to the communist narrative and a socialist realist mosaic; after 1991 the red star and worker's red book were removed.

funding: The museum sits in the state Pancasila Sakti monument complex at Lubang Buaya and is jointly managed by the Indonesian Military (TNI) and the Education and Culture Ministry. It was built by the TNI History Centre, initiated by Brigadier General Nugroho Notosusanto and approved by President Suharto. Admission is 5,000 rupiah.
note: Opened by President Suharto on 1 October 1992 with 34 dioramas; it draws tens of thousands of visitors a year, mostly school groups, and a new wing opened in 2013.

propaganda.summary: Suharto's Army History Centre opened the museum in 1992; its 34 dioramas present the New Order account of PKI treachery in 1965 and omit the mass killings that followed.

funding: The 12 million dollar memorial was paid for mostly by Phnom Penh Municipal Hall, with the remainder donated by tycoon Ly Yong Phat, who also gave the land. The Win-Win Monument Construction Committee, headed by General Nem Sowath, runs the site and its museum. The Defence Ministry solicited public donations during construction.
note: Inaugurated by Hun Sen on 29 December 2018 on an 8 hectare plaza in Chroy Changvar; the 33 metre monolith stands on a base with bas-reliefs, and the museum covers Hun Sen's achievements.

propaganda.summary: Hun Sen's government built the memorial, opened 2018, to honour his win-win policy; carvings depict his political triumphs including the 2017 dissolution of the opposition CNRP, and the museum shows his achievements.

funding: The hall was established by a joint decision of the CCP Central Committee, the NPC Standing Committee, the State Council and the Central Military Commission on 8 October 1976. It is described by the Party as the highest memorial hall of the Party and state and a national patriotic education demonstration base. Entry is free.
note: Opened 9 September 1977 in Tiananmen Square; it has received nearly 240 million visitors and over 190 foreign heads of state, with memorial rooms for Mao, Zhou Enlai, Liu Shaoqi, Zhu De, Deng Xiaoping and Chen Yun.

propaganda.summary: The Party and state built the hall in 1976 to 1977 to display Mao's embalmed body; the Party designates it a national patriotic education demonstration base.

n: Hong Kong Museum of the War of Resistance and Coastal Defence
funding: The museum is owned and run by the Hong Kong Government's Leisure and Cultural Services Department. The HKSAR Government describes it as one of its important cultivation bases for promoting patriotism. Admission to its thematic exhibitions is free.
note: Housed in the 1887 British Lei Yue Mun Fort, opened in 2000 as the Museum of Coastal Defence and renamed on 3 September 2024 by Chief Executive John Lee; its permanent exhibition has 11 galleries.

propaganda.summary: The 2023 Policy Address ordered the Museum of Coastal Defence converted to strengthen national pride and patriotism; the government renamed it on 3 September 2024 as a patriotic education base.

funding: The museum is owned by the Spanish General State Administration and is one of the national museums attached to the Ministry of Culture. Its directing bodies have depended on the Ministry of Education and later Culture since its creation. Contact runs through the cultura.gob.es domain.
note: Created by decree on 19 April 1941, shown provisionally in the National Archaeological Museum from 1944; its Ciudad Universitaria building was partly inaugurated on 12 October 1965 and fully reopened in 1994.

propaganda.summary: Franco's Ministry of Education created the museum by decree in 1941 within the Hispanidad ideology; its decree said it should inspire Spaniards and its displays presented conquest and colonisation as a civilising, evangelising project.

funding: Fondazione La Quadriennale di Roma is funded by its partners: the Ministry of Culture, Roma Capitale's Department of Culture, the Lazio Region and the Rome Chamber of Commerce. It is based at Villa Carpegna, which also houses the ARBIQ archive of Italian contemporary art. The Lazio Region lists it among its grandi fondazioni.
note: Founded by resolution of the Governorate of Rome in 1927 and first held in 1931 at the Palazzo delle Esposizioni; it became an autonomous body by royal decree in 1937.

propaganda.summary: Under Cipriano Efisio Oppo the 1931 to 1943 Quadriennali built consensus for the fascist regime; the 1935 halls celebrated regime policies and Mussolini, and the 1939 edition ran under ministerial supervision and racial laws.

funding: Since 1 June 2024 the memorial is the property of the Czech Ministry of Defence, administered by the Military History Institute Prague. From 2000 to 2024 it was administered by the National Museum, which renovated it and ran the exhibitions Laboratory of Power and Crossroads of Czech and Czechoslovak Statehood. State ceremonies and military parades are held there.
note: Built 1928 to 1938 by architect Jan Zázvorka to honour Czechoslovak legionaries, with the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and Bohumil Kafka's equestrian statue of Jan Žižka; the former mausoleum is now closed to the public.

propaganda.summary: After 1948 the Communist Party made the memorial its pantheon; the Central Committee opened the Klement Gottwald Mausoleum there in December 1953, run by an Interior Ministry department until the body was cremated in 1962.

funding: The museum is a Portuguese state museum. In 2019 it operated under the Directorate-General for Cultural Heritage (DGPC) as a twin pole of the Museu Nacional de Etnologia, and in 2023 Decree-Law 79/2023 transferred DGPC's management of national museums to Museus e Monumentos de Portugal E.P.E., supervised by the ministers of finance and culture. Admission is 5 euros.
note: Occupies the adapted popular life pavilion of the 1940 Portuguese World Exhibition in Belém with 1948 murals; closed in 2003, it reopened at reduced scale in December 2016 after a citizens' campaign.

propaganda.summary: The Estado Novo's SNI opened the museum in July 1948 from the 1940 exhibition's Centro Regional; the SNI managed it directly and its rural ethnographic vision of national identity served António Ferro's política do espírito.
